prompt:
Consider the sequence $s_1, s_2, s_3, \ldots$ of positive integers defined by

* $s_1 = 2$, and
* for each positive integer $n$, $s_{n+1}$ is equal to $s_n$ plus the product of the prime factors of $s_n$.

The first terms of the sequence are $2, 4, 6, 12, 18, 24$.

Prove that the product of the $2019$ smallest primes is a term of the sequence.
answer: By induction every primorial $P_k=p_1\cdots p_k$ occurs: from $P_k$ the sequence runs $2P_k,3P_k,\dots$ until the first multiplier with a new prime factor, which is $p_{k+1}$.

solutions.title: Induction on primorials
solutions.body:
Let $p_1<p_2<\cdots$ be the primes and $P_k=p_1p_2\cdots p_k$. For a positive integer $x$ write $\operatorname{rad}(x)$ for the product of its distinct prime factors, so $s_{n+1}=s_n+\operatorname{rad}(s_n)$. We prove by induction that **every** $P_k$ is a term; $k=2019$ is the required statement.

**Base.** $P_1=2=s_1$.

**Step.** Suppose $s_N=P_k$. We claim $s_{N+j-1}=jP_k$ for $j=1,2,\dots,p_{k+1}$. This holds for $j=1$. If $s_{N+j-1}=jP_k$ with $1\le j<p_{k+1}$, then every prime factor of $j$ is at most $j<p_{k+1}$, hence is one of $p_1,\dots,p_k$. So the distinct prime factors of $jP_k$ are exactly $p_1,\dots,p_k$, i.e. $\operatorname{rad}(jP_k)=P_k$, and
$$s_{N+j}=jP_k+P_k=(j+1)P_k .$$
Taking $j=p_{k+1}$ gives the term $p_{k+1}P_k=P_{k+1}$.

By induction all $P_k$ are terms, in particular the product of the $2019$ smallest primes. ∎

(Check: $2\to4\to6=P_2\to12\to18\to24\to30=P_3\to60\to\cdots$.)

prompt:
Consider the operation $*$ that takes a pair of integers and returns an integer according to the rule
$$a * b = a \times (b + 1).$$

(a) For each positive integer $n$, determine all permutations $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_n$ of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ that maximise the value of
$$(\cdots((a_1 * a_2) * a_3) * \cdots * a_{n-1}) * a_n.$$

(b) For each positive integer $n$, determine all permutations $b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_n$ of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ that maximise the value of
$$b_1 * (b_2 * (b_3 * \cdots * (b_{n-1} * b_n) \cdots)).$$
answer: (a) Exactly the permutations with $a_1=n$ (all $(n-1)!$ of them). (b) Only the decreasing permutation $n,n-1,\dots,2,1$.

solutions.title: Closed forms, then compare
solutions.body:
**(a)** By induction on $n$,
$$(\cdots((a_1*a_2)*a_3)*\cdots)*a_n=a_1(a_2+1)(a_3+1)\cdots(a_n+1),$$
since applying $*\,a_{k}$ multiplies the current value by $a_k+1$. For a permutation of $\{1,\dots,n\}$,
$$a_1\prod_{i=2}^n(a_i+1)=\frac{a_1}{a_1+1}\prod_{i=1}^n(a_i+1)=\frac{a_1}{a_1+1}\,(n+1)! .$$
This depends only on $a_1$ and is strictly increasing in $a_1$, so it is maximal exactly when $a_1=n$.

**Answer (a):** all permutations with $a_1=n$ (the order of the other numbers is arbitrary).

**(b)** By induction from the inside out,
$$b_1*(b_2*(\cdots*(b_{n-1}*b_n)\cdots))=b_1+b_1b_2+b_1b_2b_3+\cdots+b_1b_2\cdots b_n .$$
Indeed, if the inner expression $b_2*(\cdots)$ equals $b_2+b_2b_3+\cdots+b_2\cdots b_n$, then multiplying (inner $+1$) by $b_1$ gives the formula. (For $n=1$ the expression is just $b_1$.)

Suppose $b_i<b_{i+1}$ for some $i$, and let $c$ be the permutation obtained by swapping $b_i$ and $b_{i+1}$. All products $b_1\cdots b_j$ with $j\ne i$ are unchanged, so
$$\text{value}(c)-\text{value}(b)=b_1\cdots b_{i-1}\,b_{i+1}-b_1\cdots b_{i-1}\,b_i=b_1\cdots b_{i-1}(b_{i+1}-b_i)>0 .$$
Hence a maximising permutation (one exists, as there are finitely many) has no ascent, so it is decreasing.

**Answer (b):** only $b=(n,n-1,\dots,2,1)$. ∎

prompt:
For some positive integer $n$, a coin will be flipped $n$ times to obtain a sequence of $n$ heads and tails. For each flip of the coin, there is probability $p$ of obtaining a head and probability $1 - p$ of obtaining a tail, where $0 < p < 1$ is a rational number.

Kim writes all $2^n$ possible sequences of $n$ heads and tails in two columns, with some sequences in the left column and the remaining sequences in the right column. Kim would like the sequence produced by the coin flips to appear in the left column with probability $\frac12$.

Determine all pairs $(n, p)$ for which this is possible.
answer: Exactly the pairs $(n,\tfrac12)$, $n\ge1$ (rational root theorem forces $p=1/m$ and, by symmetry, $1-p=1/m'$).

solutions.title: Rational root theorem twice
solutions.body:
**Answer: all pairs $(n,\frac12)$ with $n\ge1$.**

**$p=\frac12$ works:** put all sequences starting with a head in the left column.

**Necessity.** A sequence with $k$ heads has probability $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. If the left column contains $a_k$ sequences with $k$ heads ($0\le a_k\le\binom nk$, integers), the requirement is
$$F(p):=2\sum_{k=0}^n a_k\,p^k(1-p)^{n-k}-1=0 .$$
$F$ is a polynomial in $p$ with integer coefficients and constant term $F(0)=2a_0-1=\pm1$ (as $a_0\in\{0,1\}$). By the rational root theorem, a rational root $p=\frac rs$ in lowest terms has $r\mid \pm1$, so $p=\frac1m$ for an integer $m\ge2$.

Now exchange the roles of heads and tails: in terms of $q=1-p$, the same equation reads $2\sum_k a_k(1-q)^kq^{n-k}-1=0$, a polynomial in $q$ with integer coefficients and constant term $2a_n-1=\pm1$ (as $a_n\in\{0,1\}$). So also $1-p=\frac1{m'}$ for an integer $m'\ge2$.

Then $\frac1m+\frac1{m'}=1$ with $m,m'\ge2$, which forces $m=m'=2$, i.e. $p=\frac12$. ∎

solutions.title: Reduce modulo $m-1$ (official route, corrected)
solutions.body:
As in the first approach, the rational root theorem gives $p=\frac1m$ with $m\ge2$ an integer. Substituting, $p^k(1-p)^{n-k}=\frac{(m-1)^{n-k}}{m^n}$, so the condition becomes
$$2\sum_{k=0}^n a_k(m-1)^{n-k}=m^n .$$
Reduce modulo $m-1$: every term with $k<n$ contains the factor $m-1$, and $m\equiv1$, so $2a_n\equiv1\pmod{m-1}$. Since $a_n\in\{0,1\}$, $m-1$ divides $2a_n-1=\pm1$, so $m=2$ and $p=\frac12$.

(The official solution writes $2a_0-1$ at this point; it is the coefficient $a_n$ of the all-heads sequence that survives modulo $m-1$.) Conversely $p=\frac12$ works for every $n$. ∎

prompt:
Suppose that $x_1, x_2, x_3, \ldots$ is a strictly decreasing sequence of positive real numbers such that the series $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 + \cdots$ diverges.

Is it necessarily true that the series
$$\sum_{n=2}^{\infty} \min\left\{x_n, \frac{1}{n \log n}\right\}$$
diverges?

solutions.title: A block-constant counterexample
solutions.body:
**Answer: no.** We construct a counterexample ($\log$ is the natural logarithm; the base does not matter).

**Reduction to non-increasing sequences.** If $(x_n)$ is non-increasing, positive, with $\sum x_n=\infty$ and $\sum\min\{x_n,\frac1{n\log n}\}<\infty$, then $y_n=x_n+2^{-n}$ is strictly decreasing, $\sum y_n=\infty$, and $\min\{y_n,c\}\le\min\{x_n,c\}+2^{-n}$, so $\sum\min\{y_n,\frac1{n\log n}\}<\infty$ as well.

**The construction.** Let $M_0=1$ and $M_k=\lceil e^{e^k}\rceil$ for $k\ge1$ (so $M_1=16$, $M_2=1619,\dots$); note $\log M_k\ge e^k$ and $M_k\ge2M_{k-1}$. Define
$$x_n=\frac1{M_k}\qquad\text{for } M_{k-1}<n\le M_k .$$
This is positive and non-increasing.

**$\sum x_n$ diverges:** block $k$ contributes $\frac{M_k-M_{k-1}}{M_k}\ge\frac12$.

**$\sum\min$ converges.** Fix $k\ge2$ and split block $k$ into $I_k=\{n: n\log n\le M_k\}$ and $J_k=\{n:n\log n>M_k\}$.

* On $I_k$, $\min\le x_n=\frac1{M_k}$. Elements $n\ge\sqrt{M_k}$ of $I_k$ satisfy $\log n\ge\frac12\log M_k$, hence $n\le\frac{2M_k}{\log M_k}$. So $|I_k|\le\sqrt{M_k}+\frac{2M_k}{\log M_k}$ and the contribution is at most $M_k^{-1/2}+\frac2{\log M_k}\le e^{-e^k/2}+2e^{-k}$.
* On $J_k$, $\min\le\frac1{n\log n}$, and $n>\frac{M_k}{\log n}\ge\frac{M_k}{\log M_k}=:L_k$. Since $t\mapsto\frac1{t\log t}$ is decreasing with antiderivative $\log\log t$,
$$\sum_{n\in J_k}\frac1{n\log n}\le\frac1{L_k\log L_k}+\int_{L_k}^{M_k}\frac{dt}{t\log t}=\frac1{L_k\log L_k}-\log\Big(1-\frac{\log\log M_k}{\log M_k}\Big).$$
With $u_k=\frac{\log\log M_k}{\log M_k}$: the function $\frac{\log s}{s}$ is decreasing for $s\ge e$ and $\log M_k\ge e^k$, so $u_k\le ke^{-k}\le\frac12$; and $-\log(1-u)\le2u$ for $0\le u\le\frac12$. Also $\log L_k\ge1$ and $\log M_k\le e^k+1$, so $\frac1{L_k\log L_k}\le\frac{\log M_k}{M_k}\le(e^k+1)e^{-e^k}$. The contribution of $J_k$ is therefore at most $(e^k+1)e^{-e^k}+2ke^{-k}$.

Both bounds are summable over $k$ (e.g. $\sum_k ke^{-k}<\infty$), and block $1$ is finite, so $\sum_{n\ge2}\min\{x_n,\frac1{n\log n}\}<\infty$.

After the perturbation $y_n=x_n+2^{-n}$ we get a strictly decreasing positive sequence with $\sum y_n=\infty$ but $\sum\min\{y_n,\frac1{n\log n}\}<\infty$. So the answer is **no**. ∎

*Idea in one line:* $x_n$ is constant ($=1/M_k$) on huge blocks; $\frac1{n\log n}$ is smaller only at the end of a block, where $\sum\frac1{n\log n}$ over $[M_k/\log M_k,M_k]$ is only about $\frac{\log\log M_k}{\log M_k}$. (The official solution uses the same idea with blocks ending at $a_k\log a_k$.)

prompt:
Determine all pairs $(a, b)$ of real numbers with $a \le b$ that maximise the integral
$$\int_a^b e^{\cos x}\left(380 - x - x^2\right) \mathrm{d}x.$$
answer: Only $(a,b)=(-20,19)$ — exactly the interval where the integrand is positive.

solutions.title: Integrate exactly over the positive part
solutions.body:
**Answer: $(a,b)=(-20,19)$ only.**

Write the integrand as $f(x)=e^{\cos x}(380-x-x^2)=-e^{\cos x}(x+20)(x-19)$. It is continuous, and since $e^{\cos x}>0$:
$$f>0\ \text{on }(-20,19),\qquad f<0\ \text{on }(-\infty,-20)\cup(19,\infty).$$
We use repeatedly: if $f>0$ on an interval $(u,v)$ with $u<v$, then $\int_u^vf>0$; similarly with $<$.

Let $I(a,b)=\int_a^bf$. Then $I(-20,19)>0$. Take any $a\le b$.

* If $a\ge19$ or $b\le-20$, the interval lies where $f\le0$, so $I(a,b)\le0<I(-20,19)$.
* Otherwise $a<19$ and $b>-20$, and
$$I(-20,19)-I(a,b)=\int_b^{19}f+\int_{-20}^{a}f .$$
The first integral is $0$ if $b=19$ and positive otherwise: for $-20<b<19$ the integrand is positive on $(b,19)$, and for $b>19$ we have $\int_b^{19}f=-\int_{19}^bf>0$. Likewise the second integral is $0$ if $a=-20$ and positive otherwise: for $-20<a<19$ it is $\int_{-20}^af>0$, and for $a<-20$ it is $-\int_a^{-20}f>0$.

So $I(a,b)\le I(-20,19)$ with equality if and only if $a=-20$ and $b=19$. ∎

(Numerically the maximum is $\approx 1.2457\times10^4$.)

prompt:
For each odd prime $p$, prove that the integer
$$1! + 2! + 3! + \cdots + p! - \left\lfloor \frac{(p-1)!}{e} \right\rfloor$$
is divisible by $p$.

(Here, $e$ denotes the base of the natural logarithm and $\lfloor x \rfloor$ denotes the largest integer that is less than or equal to $x$.)
answer: $\left\lfloor\frac{(p-1)!}{e}\right\rfloor=\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}$, and $(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}\equiv(p-1-k)!\pmod p$, so the floor is $\equiv1!+\cdots+(p-1)!$.

solutions.title: Series for $1/e$ and Wilson-type congruences
solutions.body:
**Step 1: the floor exactly.** From $e^{-1}=\sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}$,
$$\frac{(p-1)!}{e}=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}\;+\;(-1)^p\Big(\frac1p-\frac1{p(p+1)}+\frac1{p(p+1)(p+2)}-\cdots\Big).$$
The terms with $k\le p-1$ are integers. The bracket is an alternating series with decreasing terms tending to $0$, so its value lies strictly between $\frac1p-\frac1{p(p+1)}>0$ and $\frac1p<1$. As $p$ is odd, $(-1)^p=-1$, so $\frac{(p-1)!}{e}$ equals the integer $\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}$ minus a number in $(0,1)$. Hence
$$\Big\lfloor\frac{(p-1)!}{e}\Big\rfloor=\sum_{k=0}^{p-1}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}-1=\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!},$$
because the $k=p-1$ term is $(-1)^{p-1}=1$.

**Step 2: reduce mod $p$.** For $0\le k\le p-2$,
$$\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}=(k+1)(k+2)\cdots(p-1)\equiv(-1)^{p-1-k}(p-1-k)(p-2-k)\cdots1=(-1)^{p-1-k}(p-1-k)!\pmod p,$$
using $j\equiv-(p-j)$. Since $p-1$ is even, $(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}\equiv(-1)^{p-1}(p-1-k)!=(p-1-k)!$. Summing over $k=0,\dots,p-2$,
$$\Big\lfloor\frac{(p-1)!}{e}\Big\rfloor\equiv\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}(p-1-k)!=1!+2!+\cdots+(p-1)!\pmod p .$$

**Conclusion.** $1!+\cdots+p!-\lfloor(p-1)!/e\rfloor\equiv p!\equiv0\pmod p$. ∎

solutions.title: Same floor, congruence via inverses (official route)
solutions.body:
Step 1 is as in the first approach: $\lfloor (p-1)!/e\rfloor=\sum_{k=0}^{p-2}(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}$.

For $0\le k\le p-1$, $k!=1\cdot2\cdots k\equiv(1-p)(2-p)\cdots(k-p)=(-1)^k(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)\pmod p$. Every factor is invertible mod $p$, so in the field $\mathbb Z/p\mathbb Z$
$$(-1)^k\frac{(p-1)!}{k!}\equiv\frac{(p-1)!}{(p-1)(p-2)\cdots(p-k)}=(p-1-k)! .$$
Summing over $0\le k\le p-2$ gives $\lfloor (p-1)!/e\rfloor\equiv (p-1)!+(p-2)!+\cdots+1!$, and since $p!\equiv0$, the given integer is divisible by $p$. ∎

(Check: $p=3$: $1+2+6-\lfloor 2/e\rfloor=9-0=9$; $p=5$: $153-\lfloor24/e\rfloor=153-8=145=5\cdot29$.)

prompt:
Let $G$ be a finite simple graph and let $k$ be the largest number of vertices of any clique in $G$. Suppose that we label each vertex of $G$ with a non-negative real number, so that the sum of all such labels is $1$. Define the *value of an edge* to be the product of the labels of the two vertices at its ends. Define the *value of a labelling* to be the sum of the values of the edges.

Prove that the maximum possible value of a labelling of $G$ is $\frac{k-1}{2k}$.

(A *finite simple graph* is a graph with finitely many vertices, in which each edge connects two distinct vertices and no two edges connect the same two vertices. A *clique* in a graph is a set of vertices in which any two are connected by an edge.)
answer: Uniform labels $\frac1k$ on a maximum clique give $\frac{k-1}{2k}$; conversely, shifting weight between non-adjacent vertices never decreases the value, until the support is a clique, where the value is $\frac12(1-\sum a_i^2)\le\frac12(1-\frac1t)$ (Motzkin–Straus).

solutions.title: Shift weight onto a clique
solutions.body:
**The value $\frac{k-1}{2k}$ is attained.** Label the $k$ vertices of a largest clique with $\frac1k$ and all others with $0$. The $\binom k2$ clique edges each have value $\frac1{k^2}$ and all other edges have value $0$, so the value is $\frac{k(k-1)}2\cdot\frac1{k^2}=\frac{k-1}{2k}$.

**No labelling does better.** Let $x$ be any labelling and $V(x)$ its value.

*Shifting step.* Suppose $u,v$ are **non-adjacent** vertices with labels $a,b>0$. Let $S_u$, $S_v$ be the sums of the labels of the neighbours of $u$ and of $v$ (neither includes $a$ or $b$, as $u,v$ are not adjacent); by symmetry $S_u\ge S_v$. The edges at $u$ or $v$ contribute $aS_u+bS_v$, and no edge contains both. Changing the labels to $a+b$ at $u$ and $0$ at $v$ keeps the total $1$, leaves all other edge values unchanged, and the contribution becomes $(a+b)S_u\ge aS_u+bS_v$. So $V$ does not decrease.

Each step increases the number of vertices labelled $0$, so after finitely many steps we reach a labelling $x'$ with $V(x')\ge V(x)$ in which any two vertices with positive labels are adjacent. These vertices form a clique, so their number $t$ satisfies $1\le t\le k$. With their labels $a_1,\dots,a_t$ (summing to $1$), only edges inside this clique have non-zero value, and all its pairs are edges, so
$$V(x')=\sum_{i<j}a_ia_j=\frac12\Big(\big(\textstyle\sum a_i\big)^2-\sum a_i^2\Big)=\frac12\Big(1-\sum a_i^2\Big).$$
By the QM–AM (or Cauchy–Schwarz) inequality, $\sum a_i^2\ge\frac1t\big(\sum a_i\big)^2=\frac1t$. Hence
$$V(x)\le V(x')\le\frac12-\frac1{2t}\le\frac12-\frac1{2k}=\frac{k-1}{2k}.$$

So the maximum value of a labelling is exactly $\frac{k-1}{2k}$. ∎ (This is the Motzkin–Straus theorem.)

prompt:
*The following problem is open in the sense that no solution is currently known to part (b). A proof of part (a) will be awarded 3 points.*

A *binary string* is a sequence, each of whose terms is $0$ or $1$. A set $\mathcal B$ of binary strings is defined inductively according to the following rules.

* The binary string $1$ is in $\mathcal B$.
* If $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$ is in $\mathcal B$ with $n$ odd, then both $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n, 0$ and $0, s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$ are in $\mathcal B$.
* If $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$ is in $\mathcal B$ with $n$ even, then both $s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n, 1$ and $1, s_1, s_2, \ldots, s_n$ are in $\mathcal B$.
* No other binary strings are in $\mathcal B$.

For each positive integer $n$, let $b_n$ be the number of binary strings in $\mathcal B$ of length $n$.

(a) Prove that there exist constants $c_1, c_2 > 0$ and $1.6 < \lambda_1, \lambda_2 < 1.9$ such that $c_1\lambda_1^n < b_n < c_2\lambda_2^n$ for all positive integers $n$.

(b) Determine $\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{b_n}$ and $\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty} \sqrt[n]{b_n}$.
answer: (a) $\lambda_1=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2$ (strings with different end digits satisfy $a_{n+1}\ge a_n+a_{n-1}$) and $\lambda_2=\psi\approx1.839$, the real root of $x^3=x^2+x+1$ (move words avoiding $RRLL$). (b) is an **open problem**.

solutions.title: Part (a): Fibonacci from below, tribonacci from above
solutions.body:
A string of length $n$ in $\mathcal B$ is extended by the digit $d_n$ ($d_n=0$ if $n$ is odd, $1$ if $n$ is even) on the left ($L$) or on the right ($R$); call these *moves*. Every string of length $n$ in $\mathcal B$ arises from $1$ by $n-1$ moves. Let $\mathcal B_n$ be the strings of length $n$, so $b_n=|\mathcal B_n|$.

**Lower bound, $\lambda_1=\varphi=\frac{1+\sqrt5}2\approx1.618$.** Let $\mathcal A_n\subseteq\mathcal B_n$ be the strings whose first and last digits differ and $a_n=|\mathcal A_n|$. Directly: $\mathcal B_2=\{10,01\}$, $\mathcal B_3=\{101,110,011\}$, so $a_2=a_3=2$.

For $n\ge3$ define $f:\mathcal A_n\cup\mathcal A_{n-1}\to\mathcal A_{n+1}$:
* For $s\in\mathcal A_n$: exactly one end of $s$ equals $d_n$; let $f(s)$ be $s$ with $d_n$ added at **that** end. The new ends differ again, and $f(s)$ starts or ends with a repeated pair $d_nd_n$.
* For $s=x\,t\,y\in\mathcal A_{n-1}$ ($x\ne y$ digits): apply the two moves (digits $d_{n-1}$ then $d_n=1-d_{n-1}$) so as to put $y$ on the left and $x$ on the right: $f(s)=y\,x\,t\,y\,x$ (if $d_{n-1}=x$ add it on the right first, otherwise add $y$ on the left first). Its ends $y\ne x$ differ, and neither end is a repeated pair.

$f$ is injective on $\mathcal A_n$ (delete the end digit equal to $d_n$ — the other end differs from it) and on $\mathcal A_{n-1}$ (delete both ends), and the two images are disjoint (repeated end pair or not). Hence
$$a_{n+1}\ge a_n+a_{n-1}\qquad(n\ge3).$$
With $F_1=F_2=1$ the Fibonacci numbers, induction gives $a_n\ge2F_{n-1}$ for $n\ge2$, and $F_m\ge\varphi^{m-2}$ (as $F_{m+1}\ge\varphi^{m-2}+\varphi^{m-3}=\varphi^{m-1}$). So for $n\ge2$, $b_n\ge a_n\ge2\varphi^{n-3}>\varphi^{-3}\varphi^n$, and $b_1=1>\varphi^{-3}\varphi$. Take $c_1=\varphi^{-3}$, $\lambda_1=\varphi\in(1.6,1.9)$.

**Upper bound, $\lambda_2=\psi\approx1.839$**, the real root of $p(x)=x^3-x^2-x-1$. Since $p'(x)=3x^2-2x-1>0$ for $x>1$, $p(1)<0$, $p(1.8)=-0.208<0$ and $p(1.9)=0.349>0$, $p$ has exactly one root $\psi>1$, and $1.8<\psi<1.9$.

*Commutation.* From any string of length $m$, the moves $RRLL$ and $LLRR$ give the same result: the added digits are $u,v,u,v$ with $v=1-u$, and both orders produce $v\,u\,s\,u\,v$. Replacing an occurrence of $RRLL$ by $LLRR$ in a move word strictly decreases the sum of the positions of the $L$s, so after finitely many replacements every string of $\mathcal B_n$ is produced by a word of length $n-1$ over $\{L,R\}$ **avoiding $RRLL$**. Hence $b_n\le d_{n-1}$, where $d_m$ is the number of such words of length $m$.

*Counting $d_m$.* $d_0,d_1,d_2,d_3=1,2,4,8$. For $m\ge3$, a word of length $m+1$ avoiding $RRLL$ is a word $w$ of length $m$ avoiding it plus a letter; $wR$ is always fine, $wL$ fails exactly when $w$ ends in $RRL$, and words $w'RRL$ of length $m$ (avoiding $RRLL$) correspond to arbitrary valid $w'$ of length $m-3$. So $d_{m+1}=2d_m-d_{m-3}$. Then $e_m=d_m-d_{m-1}$ satisfies $e_{m+1}=d_m-d_{m-3}=e_m+e_{m-1}+e_{m-2}$ (tribonacci), with $e_1,e_2,e_3=1,2,4$. As $1\le\psi$, $2\le\psi^2$, $4\le\psi^3$ and $\psi^3=\psi^2+\psi+1$, induction gives $e_m\le\psi^m$. Therefore
$$b_n\le d_{n-1}=1+\sum_{j=1}^{n-1}e_j\le1+\frac{\psi^n-\psi}{\psi-1}=\frac{\psi^n-1}{\psi-1}<\frac{\psi^n}{0.8}<2\psi^n .$$
Take $c_2=2$, $\lambda_2=\psi\in(1.6,1.9)$.

This proves (a): $\varphi^{-3}\varphi^n<b_n<2\psi^n$ for all $n\ge1$. ∎

**Part (b) is an open problem.** Part (a) shows $\varphi\le\liminf\sqrt[n]{b_n}\le\limsup\sqrt[n]{b_n}\le\psi$. Numerically, $b_1,b_2,\dots=1,2,3,5,9,16,29,52,94,170,308,560,\dots$, and the ratio $b_{n+1}/b_n$ is about $1.83$ for $n\approx23$ (slowly increasing), but the exact growth rate is not known.
